title: The Great Smoking Divide
author: Ellen Meara, Harvard Chan School
summary: Research from Harvard, Dartmouth, UPenn, and Federal Reserve Bank of Boston reveals tobacco use as the strongest predictor of mortality differences between American regions and education groups. The mortality gap widened from 2.6 to 6.3 years between 1992 and 2019. While "deaths of despair" receive attention, smoking patterns better explain rural-urban health divides and structural health inequalities. Smoking indicates underlying structural factors affecting both tobacco use and premature death.
points: Smoking strongest predictor of mortality gaps between regions (not deaths of despair)
Mortality gap widened from 2.6 years (1992) to 6.3 years (2019)
Rural areas historically healthiest now experiencing shortest lifespans
Smoking serves as marker for communities experiencing structural decline
Deaths of despair insufficient explanation for observed health inequalities
quotes: Smoking emerges as an exceptionally powerful predictor of mortality trends.

We are very interested in rural-urban differences. Historically, rural areas were always healthier. This is part of the tragedy. We took the healthiest parts of the country — in a country as rich as ours — and not only are they not enjoying the same gains in longevity, but they're seeing shorter lives.

Smoking is a very effective marker for where places are struggling, that's why we're trying to understand the underlying factors that may explain strong links between smoking and deaths in those areas.” Archived from Harvard Gazette on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
